report.summary:
Here's what I've learned about you. You started Southside Youth Peace Collective in 2023, and you are now in your third year. You run street outreach and youth mentoring with a team of 4, and two of them are full time. Young people and families trust you. That trust is your greatest asset. Right now, most of the back-office work runs through you and the founder. Your funding is one city contract plus small individual gifts.

You are strong in the things that keep a young group going. Your answers show you already use an accounting system, you share financial duties, and you build an annual budget. You track basic activities like people served and services delivered. You have someone responsible for data. You also have a base of supporters, you bring in money beyond donated time and space, and you know where funding will come from for the next 6 to 12 months. That is a real foundation.

You have room to grow in writing down your plans, in making sure cash is there for payroll every time, and in building a wider and steadier base of funding. Across planning, money, fundraising and tracking results, your answers place you at the Seeding stage. That is normal for a group this age. It also means small steps can make a big difference. Many of these areas lift each other. A written plan makes it easier to track results, and tracked results make it easier to ask funders for more.

If I were you, I would start with two things. First, write one simple work plan that says your goals, activities, deadlines and who owns each task. Second, look closely at your cash flow so you know payroll is safe. With one city contract, a late payment could hit your team fast. These two steps protect your people and open the door to everything else. Go one step at a time. You do not have to fix everything at once.

report.summary:
Esto es lo que he aprendido sobre ti. Southside Youth Peace Collective tiene tres años de trabajo en su barrio, con interrupción de violencia y mentoría para jóvenes. Eres un equipo de 4 personas y, según el perfil, casi todo el trabajo de oficina pasa por ti y por el fundador. Eso es mucho peso. Tu mayor tesoro es la confianza que tienes con los jóvenes y las familias, y eso no se compra ni se improvisa.

Eres fuerte en lo básico que ya funciona. Tienes un sistema de contabilidad, un presupuesto anual y responsabilidades financieras compartidas. También cuentas con apoyo de personas que donan, subvenciones de $10,000 o más, claridad sobre el dinero de los próximos 6 a 12 meses, y una persona encargada de los datos. Tus respuestas muestran que las cuatro áreas revisadas (planificación, recaudación de fondos, manejo del dinero y aprendizaje con datos) están en la etapa inicial, llamada "Semilla". Es normal en una organización joven. Es un punto de partida, no un juicio sobre tu trabajo.

Tienes espacio para crecer en poner por escrito lo que ya sabes, en asegurar que el dinero llegue a tiempo para pagar al equipo, y en tener más de una fuente de ingresos además del contrato de la ciudad. Si yo fuera tú, empezaría por dos cosas. Primero, un plan de trabajo escrito y corto. Segundo, un calendario sencillo de dinero que entra y sale, para proteger los pagos de nómina. Con esas dos bases, lo demás (fondos, datos, informes) se hace más fácil.

report.summary:
Esto es lo que he aprendido sobre usted y su organización. Riverbend Violence Interruption Network lleva desde 2016 haciendo un trabajo muy difícil: intervención en hospitales y trabajo de calle en dos precintos. Con 19 personas y un presupuesto cercano a los 2.1 millones de dólares, ya tienen sistemas que funcionan y que el equipo usa. Casi todo su dinero (alrededor del 80%) viene de fondos del gobierno que solo se pueden usar para cosas específicas. Eso es común en este campo, y también es lo que más pesa sobre su estabilidad.

Usted es fuerte en varias cosas. Sus respuestas muestran que tienen planes de trabajo escritos que revisan con regularidad. Tienen un plan escrito para conseguir fondos y una mezcla de fondos de varios años y fondos flexibles. Producen informes financieros que la dirección revisa, y hacen auditorías independientes cada año. También definen metas para sus programas, revisan los datos en equipo y los usan para tomar decisiones. En planificación y finanzas están en la etapa En desarrollo. En recaudación de fondos y en monitoreo y evaluación están en la etapa Emergente.

Usted tiene espacio para crecer en dos áreas que se apoyan una a la otra. La primera es tener a la vista, por escrito, de dónde vendrá el dinero de los próximos 12 meses. La segunda es que todo el personal, tanto en el hospital como en la calle, recoja los datos de la misma manera. Los datos claros ayudan a contar su historia a quienes financian, y eso abre la puerta a fondos más grandes y más flexibles. Si yo fuera usted, empezaría por estas dos prioridades de crecimiento: ver con claridad el dinero del próximo año y capacitar al equipo para recoger y usar datos de forma constante. Lo demás puede esperar a que estas dos bases estén firmes.

report.summary:
Here's what I've learned about you. You lead Southside Youth Peace Collective, a small team of 1 to 5 people in Illinois. You run street outreach and mentoring for young people, with a budget between $250K and $1M. That is a lot of responsibility for a very small team. Your answers show that you are at the Seeding stage in Planning, Fundraising, Financial Management and Monitoring, Learning and Evaluation. Seeding is where strong groups begin. It is not a grade on your work.

You are strong in some real ways. You already use an accounting system, you share financial duties, and you build an annual budget. You have supporters who give to your work, you win grants of $10,000 or more, and you can see where your money will come from for the next 6 to 12 months. You track basic activities like people served, you collect information on the people you serve, and someone on your team is responsible for data. Those are solid footings to build on.

You have room to grow in writing your plans down, in making sure payroll is steady, in getting funding that lasts more than one year, and in setting clear outcomes. In small groups these pieces tend to lift each other. If I were you, I would start with two things. First, a simple written work plan with goals, activities, a timeline and an owner. Second, a short cash plan so you can meet payroll every time. Plans and steady pay protect your staff, and funders look for both.

Your team of 19 runs hospital-based intervention and street outreach across two precincts. Your answers show that your core systems exist and are used, but they are uneven. Most of your money comes from restricted government funding, and your board is working well but is thin on finance know-how. This is a learning tool, not a grade. It shows where you are, not how good your work is.

You are strong in planning and money habits. You keep written work plans and check progress against them. You produce financial reports that leadership reviews, you track spending by program, you hold some reserves, and you complete an independent audit every year. In data, you use standard tools, review numbers as a team, and share results with funders and partners. Your stages today are Developing in Planning and Financial Management, and Emerging in Fundraising and in Monitoring, Learning and Evaluation.

You have room to grow in two places. One is funding. A lot of your budget depends on one type of money, so a clear, written view of the next 12 months, and later 2 to 3 years, would help you steady the whole team. The other is data. Your staff need shared training and simple rules so the numbers are the same from the hospital team to the street team. If I were you, I would start with two things: getting a clear picture of where your funding will come from over the next year, and training staff to collect and use data the same way. Once those are done, funding conversations and evaluation get much easier.
